title: Opening blind eyes
hook: blessings for sight, freedom, clothing and steady steps

segments.voice: Yesterday, the rooster's understanding, and the first blessing of the morning. Your line was tell day from night. What did you leave behind in the dark? Today, the eyes open. Day five hundred forty-four.

Your eyes open in the morning and the room comes back. Ceiling, curtain, the chair with yesterday's clothes on it. It takes half a second, and you've done it every day of your life. Now listen to what the prayer book calls that half second. Not waking up. Not getting going. It calls it opening the eyes of the blind. And it keeps going in that key. Sitting up becomes setting the captive free. Getting dressed becomes clothing the naked. Big words, the words of rescue, for the smallest motions of a morning.
screen: `THE ROOM COMES BACK.` → `OPENING THE EYES OF THE BLIND.` → `BIG WORDS FOR SMALL MOTIONS.`

segments.voice: The Talmud, in Berakhot, pairs each blessing with a motion. When you open your eyes: blessed are you, pokeach ivrim, who opens the eyes of the blind. When you sit up and stretch: matir asurim, who frees the bound, because a body stiff from sleep has just been let loose. When you dress: malbish arumim, who clothes the naked. When you stand up straight: zokef kefufim, who raises the bowed down. When you start to walk: who makes firm a person's steps. Where do these phrases come from? Several are lifted almost word for word from the Psalms. Psalm one hundred forty-six, in the old Jewish translation, says: "The LORD looseth the prisoners; the LORD openeth the eyes of the blind; the LORD raiseth up them that are bowed down." In the psalm, those are rescues: God lifting the people who have the least. The prayer book borrows that language for your own ordinary morning. Why? The Talmud elsewhere calls sleep a sixtieth part of death. Seen that way, every waking is a small return: from not seeing to seeing, from lying still to moving. And many people hear a second layer too. To say who opens the eyes of the blind is to remember that for some people, sight is not a given, and freedom isn't, and clothing isn't. The blessing thanks God for your morning in words that keep other people's mornings in view.
screen: `POKEACH IVRIM: WHO OPENS BLIND EYES.` · `A BLESSING FOR EACH MOTION.` · `BORROWED FROM PSALM 146.` · `YOUR MORNING, AND OTHERS' MORNINGS.` · then, large: `EYES OPENED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice one thing you can see. Settle, and breathe. Close your eyes for a few breaths and sit in the dark. Then open them slowly, as if for the first time today. Let your gaze land on one thing. A cup, a plant, a patch of light on the wall, your own hand. Look at it longer than you normally would: its color, its edges, the shadow it throws. If you pray, you can say pokeach ivrim, who opens the eyes of the blind. If not, just keep looking. The bell holds the time.
Opening blind eyes. Pokeach ivrim: the morning blessing for sight, borrowed from a psalm about rescue.
Your line: eyes opened. Today, once, stop and really look at something you pass every day, and see one detail you've never noticed. Day five hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: These blessings are part of the morning blessings said at home on waking or at the start of the morning service, and in many synagogues the leader chants them aloud while the congregation answers amen.

trapdoor: what you thought: a blessing about blindness.
what it means: thanks for the half second when your eyes open and the room comes back.
what a scholar hears: Berakhot 60b pairs each phrase with a waking motion, and several phrases (pokeach ivrim, matir asurim, zokef kefufim) are taken from Psalm 146:7–8.

sources.quoted: The LORD looseth the prisoners; the LORD openeth the eyes of the blind; the LORD raiseth up them that are bowed down.

notes: Psalm 146:7–8 quoted from JPS 1917 from memory; verify wording and punctuation exactly.
Berakhot 60b pairing of motions and blessings (sitting up = matir asurim; dressing = malbish arumim; standing = zokef kefufim); confirm.
Berakhot 57b: sleep as one sixtieth of death; confirm.
The 'second layer' (remembering those for whom sight, freedom, clothing are not given) is presented as how many people hear it, not as a classical source; confirm the framing is acceptable.
